questions.question: Define amoebiasis.
questions.solution_html:
• Amoebiasis is a parasitic infection of the intestines caused by the protozoan Entamoeba
  • histolytica. It is characterized by symptoms ranging from mild diarrhea to severe dysentery
  • with blood and mucus in the stool

questions.question: Describe the causative agent of diptheria.
questions.solution_html:
• The causative agent is Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It is a gram -positive, non-motile, club
  • shaped bacillus that typically arranges in "Chinese letter" patterns. It produces a potent
  • exotoxin that causes the characteristic pseudomembrane in the throat.

questions.question: What is swine flu? Mention its causative agent.
questions.solution_html:
• Swine flu is a respiratory disease caused by type A influenza viruses that regularly cause
  • outbreaks in pigs. The most well -known causative agent affecting humans is the H1N1 virus
  • strain.

questions.question: What is invasion?
questions.solution_html:
• Invasion refers to the process by which microorganisms enter host cells or tissues, spread
  • and establish an infection. It often involves the secretion of enzymes or proteins that break
  • down host physical barriers.

questions.question: Explain the pathogenicity and complications of brucellosis.
questions.solution_html:
• Pathogenicity: Brucella species are intracellular pathogens that survive within phagocytes
  • spreading through the lymphatic system to the liver, spleen, and bone marrow. It typically
  • causes "undulant fever."
  • Complications: Can include endocarditis, osteomyelitis (bone infection), meningitis, and
  • chronic fatigue.

questions.question: Define colonization resistance.
questions.solution_html:
• Colonization resistance is the mechanism by which the normal microflora protects the host
  • against the entry and overgrowth of exogenous pathogens by competing for nutrients and
  • attachment sites.

questions.question: Define syphilis.
questions.solution_html:
• Syphilis is a chronic, systemic sexually transmitted infection (STI) caused by the spirochete
  • bacterium Treponema pallidum. It progresses through primary, secondary, latent, and tertiary
  • stages if left untreated.

questions.solution_html:
• Leprosy (Hansen's disease) is a chronic infectious disease that primarily affects the skin

  • organism is Mycobacterium leprae.

questions.question: Describe the role of antifungal drugs in the treatment of cutaneous and systemic mycoses.
questions.solution_html:
• mycose.(Cutaneousmycoses(2marks),systemicmycoses(2marks))
  • Antifungal drugs disrupt fungal cell membranes by targeting ergosterol or cell wall synthesis.
  • For cutaneous mycoses, topical agents like clotrimazole are used to treat localized infections
  • of the skin and nails. Systemic mycoses require intravenous drugs like Amphotericin B to treat
  • life-threatening internal infections. Their primary role is to inhibit fungal growth while
  • minimizing damage to host cells
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Explain carrier state in typhoid fever and describe how carriers contribute to disease transmission.
questions.solution_html:
• disease transmission.(Definition of carriers (1marks), Mechanism of transmission - 2
  • marks, Site of persistance(1 marks))
  • A carrier is an asymptomatic person who harbors Salmonella typhi in their gallbladder after
  • recovering from typhoid. These individuals intermittently shed the bacteria through their feces
  • and urine into the environment. They contribute to disease transmission by contaminating
  • food and water, often through poor hand hygiene. Identifying and treating carriers is essential
  • for controlling community outbreaks and long-term prevention.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026
questions.final_answer: for controlling community outbreaks and long-term prevention.

questions.question: Explain in detail the mechanism of action of chloroquine and artemisinin.
questions.solution_html:
• (Mechanism of action of chloroquine (2 marks), artemisinin(2 marks)) /)
  • Chloroquine prevents the parasite from converting toxic heme into non -toxic hemozoin within
  • the food vacuole, leading to parasite poisoning. Artemisinin reacts with iron in the heme to
  • generate toxic free radicals that damage the parasite's proteins and membranes. Together
  • these mechanisms effectively clear Plasmodium parasites from the human bloodstream. Both
  • drugs are vital components in the global fight against malaria
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026
questions.final_answer: drugs are vital components in the global fight against malaria

questions.question: Discuss tuberculosis in detail.
questions.solution_html:
• Clinical features and management (2 marks))
  • Tuberculosis is a chronic airborne infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis that
  • primarily targets the lungs. It is characterized by the formation of granulomas, where bacteria
  • can remain dormant for long periods. Transmission occurs through respiratory droplets from
  • coughing or sneezing by an infected person. Treatment requires a multi -drug regimen
  • typically including Isoniazid and Rifampicin, over several months to ensure total eradication
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026
questions.final_answer: typically including Isoniazid and Rifampicin, over several months to ensure total eradication

questions.question: Explain the epidemiology ,virulence factors and pathogenesis of Haemophilus influenzae infections in the respiratory infections.
questions.solution_html:
• influenzae infections in the respiratory infections.(Epidemology (1marks),Virulence
  • factors (2 marks),Pathogenesis(1marks))
  • H. influenzae is a common respiratory pathogen whose main virulence factor is a
  • polysaccharide capsule that prevents phagocytosis. It colonizes the nasopharynx and can
  • cause local infections like sinusitis or systemic diseases like meningitis. Epidemiology shows
  • it primarily affects young children, though vaccines like Hib have drastically reduced severe
  • cases. Adhesion factors and IgA proteases also play key roles in its ability to infect human
  • mucosal surfaces.

questions.question: Describe antiretriviral therapy and its role in the management of AIDS.
questions.solution_html:
• Mechanism(2marks), Management (2 marks))
  • ART uses a combination of drugs to block different stages of the HIV life cycle, such as
  • reverse transcription and integration. This treatment suppresses the viral load to undetectable
  • levels, allowing the immune system to recover and maintain CD4 counts. While ART is not a
  • cure, it prevents the progression to AIDS and significantly reduces the risk of virus
  • transmission. Regular adherence is critical to avoid the development of drug -resistant HIV
  • strains.
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Discuss malaria as a parasitic disease of global importance ,including its biological characteristics.
questions.solution_html:
• characteristics.(Globalsignificance(2Marks),Lifecycle(2Marks))
  • Malaria is a major global health threat caused by Plasmodium parasites and transmitted by
  • the female Anopheles mosquito. It features a complex life cycle involving an asexual stage in
  • human liver and blood cells and a sexual stage in mosquitoes. The disease is biologically
  • characterized by recurring fevers and anemia due to the destruction of red blood cells. It
  • remains a significant challenge in tropical regions due to increasing drug and insecticide
  • resistance.
